topic: IQテストの構造模倣と、その数値化の愚かさを示すシステムの構築
title: The Number Machine: A Mock IQ Test That Measures Nothing
lead: This page imitates the familiar structure of an IQ test, with pattern puzzles, timed sections and a tidy final score, then takes that structure apart piece by piece. Each item shows what the format pretends to capture, what quietly shapes the result, and what no single number could ever hold. Play along, and notice how easily a person becomes a digit.

items.name: Raven's Progressive Matrices
items.text: A grid of abstract shapes with one cell missing, introduced by John C. Raven in 1938. People are surprised that a wordless puzzle is treated as a window into the mind, and many enjoy solving similar grids in puzzle books and apps.

items.name: Number series puzzle
items.text: A row of numbers where the solver must find the next term, such as 2, 4, 8, 16. What surprises people is that many sequences fit more than one rule, so the 'correct' answer depends on what the test-maker intended.

items.name: Verbal analogy (A is to B as C is to ?)
items.text: A word puzzle asking solvers to complete a relationship, like 'bird is to nest as bee is to hive'. These items once appeared on American college entrance exams, and many people still enjoy them as quick party brain-teasers.

items.name: Odd one out
items.text: A list of items where one does not belong to the group. People are often surprised that a clever reason can be found for almost any choice, and it remains a favorite in children's activity books and pub quizzes.

items.name: Mental rotation task
items.text: Solvers judge whether two drawn 3D figures are the same object turned in space, a task studied by Roger Shepard and Jacqueline Metzler in 1971. Surprisingly, response time grows with the angle of rotation, as if the mind turns the image step by step.

photo.artist: The original uploader was TeamMentalRotation at English Wiki

items.name: Vocabulary subtest
items.text: Test-takers explain what a series of increasingly rare words mean. Many are surprised that a test of 'reasoning' rewards reading habits and schooling so directly, while word lovers enjoy similar challenges in crosswords and word-of-the-day calendars.

items.name: Digit span test
items.text: An examiner reads a string of digits aloud, and the listener repeats them, sometimes backwards. It appears in the Wechsler intelligence scales, and people are often surprised how few digits most adults can hold, typically around seven.

items.name: Block design test
items.text: Test-takers arrange red-and-white patterned cubes to copy a pictured design against the clock. Developed from Samuel Kohs's blocks in the 1920s and used in Wechsler scales, it surprises people by turning a toy-like task into a timed score.

groups.name: Section B: The Machinery of Scoring

items.name: Time limits (制限時間)
items.text: Many IQ subtests are timed, so speed quietly becomes part of what counts as intelligence. People are often surprised that a correct answer given slowly can earn fewer points, or none, on some tasks.

items.name: Raw score (素点)
items.text: The raw score is simply the count of points earned on each subtest. It means little alone. It only becomes an IQ after being compared with other people's results, which surprises those who expect a direct measurement.

items.name: Norming sample (標準化サンプル)
items.text: Scores are interpreted against a reference group tested during standardization. Because average raw performance rose over decades, a pattern called the Flynn effect, tests must be renormed periodically. Your 'intelligence' therefore partly depends on when the test was normed.

items.name: Normal distribution (正規分布)
items.text: Scores are converted so they follow a bell-shaped normal distribution. Many people assume the curve is discovered in nature. In practice, test makers build and scale the test to produce it, so the shape is partly a design choice.

items.name: Standard deviation of 15 (標準偏差15)
items.text: Most modern IQ tests, including the Wechsler scales, set one standard deviation at 15 points. About two-thirds of people therefore score between 85 and 115. The number 15 is a convention, not a natural constant.

items.name: Mean of 100 (平均100)
items.text: An IQ of 100 is defined as the average of the norming sample. Early IQ was a ratio of mental age to chronological age times 100. David Wechsler's deviation IQ kept 100 as the anchor, so the average is set by definition.

items.name: Percentile rank (パーセンタイル順位)
items.text: A percentile rank shows the share of the norming group scoring at or below you. An IQ of 130 is roughly the 98th percentile. This reveals that IQ is fundamentally a ranking among people, not a measure of an amount.

items.name: Full Scale IQ (全検査IQ)
items.text: Results from many different subtests are combined into one Full Scale IQ. Psychologists often stress that the separate index scores and their uneven profile can say more about a person than the single headline number that people remember.

groups.name: Section C: Hidden Variables That Move the Score

items.name: Prior exposure to test formats
items.text: People who have already seen matrix puzzles, timed multiple-choice grids or number series often score higher simply because the format feels familiar. The surprise is that recognizing the type of question can matter as much as solving it.

items.name: Sleep the night before (sleep deprivation)
items.text: Research links poor or short sleep to weaker attention, working memory and reaction speed, which are the very skills many timed tests reward. A single restless night can lower a score that is later reported as a stable trait.

items.name: Hunger and nutrition
items.text: Being hungry or undernourished can make concentration harder and slow thinking during long sessions. People are often surprised that something as ordinary as skipping breakfast can shift results, even though the test claims to measure fixed ability.

items.name: Test anxiety
items.text: Test anxiety is the worry, racing heart and mental blanking some people feel under evaluation. It can crowd out working memory, so a capable person may score lower simply because the situation itself feels threatening.

items.name: Language of the test
items.text: When a test is given in a language that is not the taker's strongest, instructions and verbal items become harder to process. The score may then reflect language fluency rather than reasoning, a gap that translated tests do not fully remove.

items.name: Familiarity with the examiner's culture (cultural bias in testing)
items.text: Test items often assume shared everyday knowledge, objects or social conventions from the culture that designed them. Psychologists have long debated this bias, and it shows how a score can measure cultural familiarity rather than any universal capacity.

items.name: Practice and coaching (test preparation)
items.text: Practicing similar questions or receiving coaching on strategies and timing can raise scores, a pattern often called a practice effect. It surprises many that a number described as innate can be nudged upward through rehearsal.

items.name: Room noise and lighting
items.text: Distracting sounds, dim light, glare or an uncomfortable room can pull attention away from the questions. These conditions are rarely recorded alongside the score, so the final number quietly includes the environment as well as the person.

groups.name: Section D: Statistical Sleights of Hand

items.name: Standard error of measurement (confidence interval)
items.text: Every IQ score carries an error band, often several points either side. Few realize a reported 'exact' number is really a range, so two people scoring 98 and 104 may be statistically indistinguishable. Our machine displays the band.

items.name: Flynn effect
items.text: Average raw IQ test performance rose substantially across the twentieth century in many countries, forcing tests to be re-normed. The surprise: a score of 100 does not mean the same thing across generations, revealing the scale as relative, not absolute.

items.name: Restriction of range
items.text: When a sample includes only a narrow slice of people, such as admitted students, correlations between test scores and outcomes shrink or distort. People are surprised that the same test can look predictive or useless depending purely on who was measured.

items.name: Correlation does not imply causation
items.text: IQ scores correlate with income, health and schooling, but correlation alone cannot show the score causes these outcomes. Shared background factors may drive both. Our mock results page deliberately invites this leap, then labels it as a fallacy.

items.name: Reification of the g factor
items.text: Factor analysis yields a statistical summary called g, which is easily treated as a concrete thing inside the head. Stephen Jay Gould famously criticized this move as reification. The machine shows how one number gets mistaken for a real object.

items.name: Ceiling and floor effects
items.text: When a test is too easy or too hard, many scores pile up at the top or bottom limit, hiding real differences. Surprisingly, extreme IQ claims often exceed what a test can actually measure. Our mock test has an obvious ceiling.

items.name: Regression toward the mean
items.text: People with extreme scores on one test tend to score closer to average when retested, partly because chance contributed to the first result. Many mistake this for real decline or improvement. Retake our test and watch your 'genius' quietly fade.

groups.name: Section E: What the Number Cannot See

items.name: Curiosity
items.text: The urge to find out why things are the way they are. Surprisingly, it often grows from not knowing the answer, the very state a test penalizes. People feed it by tinkering, wandering, reading, and asking one more question.

items.name: Kindness
items.text: Acting for someone else's good without expecting a reward. It surprises people how much small gestures matter, like holding a door or remembering a name. No timed booklet records it, yet communities everywhere depend on it every day.

items.name: Humor
items.text: The ability to see and share what is funny. Good humor takes quick pattern-spotting, timing, and empathy for an audience, yet it never appears on a score sheet. People enjoy it in jokes, wordplay, comedy shows, and dinner tables.

items.name: Craftsmanship (shokunin, 職人)
items.text: The skill and care of a maker who refines their work over years. What surprises people is how much knowledge lives in the hands rather than in words. It shows in carpentry, pottery, cooking, and repairs done properly.

items.name: Musicality
items.text: Sensitivity to rhythm, melody, and expression in music. Many people with no formal training can keep time, harmonize, or feel when a note is off. It lives in singing together, playing instruments, dancing, and simply listening closely.

items.name: Patience
items.text: The capacity to wait, persist, or endure difficulty without giving up. A timed test actually rewards rushing, the opposite of patience. People practice it in gardening, teaching children, learning a skill slowly, and sitting with hard problems.

items.name: Problem solving
items.text: Finding a workable answer to a real situation with real limits: a leaking pipe, a tight budget, a broken plan. Surprisingly, the best solutions are often messy and improvised. People show it daily at work, at home, and in emergencies.

items.name: Active listening
items.text: Paying full attention to a speaker, reflecting back what they said, and holding off judgment. People are often surprised how rarely they truly feel heard. It is practiced by counselors, teachers, friends, and anyone patient enough to stay quiet.

items.name: Socratic method
items.text: A tradition of learning through questioning, associated with the Greek philosopher Socrates. Its surprise is that admitting what you do not know becomes the starting point of understanding. Classrooms and law schools still use it today.

items.name: Intellectual humility
items.text: Recognizing the limits of your own knowledge and being willing to change your mind. Psychologists study it as a trait distinct from raw intelligence. It shows up when someone says, plainly and without embarrassment, "I was wrong."

items.name: Undefined value
items.text: In programming, an undefined value marks a variable that exists but holds no meaningful result. It surprises people that software admits ignorance rather than guessing. Fittingly, it is the most honest score this machine can give you.

items.key: Interpretation: you are more than this page
items.name: The Mismeasure of Man
items.text: Stephen Jay Gould's 1981 book critiques the history of ranking human intelligence with a single number. Readers are often surprised by how much bias shaped early measurements. It remains widely read and debated in classrooms and book clubs.

items.name: Forest bathing (Shinrin-yoku, 森林浴)
items.text: Forest bathing is the Japanese practice of slowly spending time among trees, coined in the 1980s. Many are surprised it involves no exercise goal at all. People enjoy quiet walks, deep breathing and simply noticing light, sound and scent.
